content.chapter: Chapter 1: Al-Andalus, Spain under Islamic Rule
objectives: Say when Muslims ruled the Iberian Peninsula and what Al-Andalus means.
Name three historic cities of the region.
Use although, until and the passive “was known as” from the chapter.
Describe a place with a superlative + “had ever”.
content.pedagogy: This short opening chapter sets the frame of the whole book: a place (the Iberian Peninsula), a period (711–1492) and a judgement (the most advanced civilization the West had ever seen). A time line on the board from 711 to 1492 makes the frame visible and is reused in every later chapter.
priorKnowledge: Spain and Portugal on a map.
Past simple; the word “civilization”.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Al-Andalus is not only modern Andalusia: it was all the lands under Muslim rule, which grew smaller over time.
Muslims did not rule all of Spain for 781 years; the lands slowly got smaller after the 11th century.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: although + clause · until · was/is known as · the most … that … had ever seen
Notice (Activity 1): learners decide what “Although” does in the first long sentence.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose were known as / until / had ever seen, then rewrite with “never … as … as” and “people call it”.
Likely errors: *Although … but … · *was knew as · *the most advanced that the West has ever seen (in a past story).
Use (Activity 4): four to five sentences about a region with known as, although and until.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: an-da-LUS, i-BE-ri-an pe-NIN-su-la, gra-NA-da, SE-ville /səˈvɪl/, COR-do-ba.
Stress: ci-vi-li-ZA-tion, in-VAL-u-a-ble, au-TON-o-mous.
beforeReading: Show a map of Spain and Portugal. Ask: “Which cities do you know here? Why might Spain have Arabic place names?”
duringReading: First reading: When did Muslim rule start and end?
Mark 711, 1492 and “after the 11th century” on a board time line.
Find three cities and five fields of work (art, architecture …).
afterReading: Language Focus: although (Activity 1), known as / until / had ever (Activity 2), rewriting (Activity 3), my region (Activity 4).
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Map hook; 5–12 First reading for the dates, time line on the board; 12–18 Second reading: cities and fields of work in a two-column chart; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–34 Language Focus Activities 1–3; 34–42 Use: four to five sentences about a region, shared in pairs; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What does the chapter say made this civilization special?
Why do you think the lands got smaller after the 11th century? (The book explains later.)
Which modern Spanish cities keep this history?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “781 Years” and “Andalusia Today” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: advanced, brilliant, civilization, numerous, invaluable, autonomous.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the time line with 711 and 1492 already written and the frames “Although ____, ____.” and “____ until ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a five-sentence introduction to a museum room about Al-Andalus, using although, until and known as.

formativeAssessment: Gives 711–1492 and explains Al-Andalus correctly.
Uses although with one clause, without “but”.
Uses “was known as” as a passive.
expectedResponses: Al-Andalus was the name of the lands under Muslim rule in the Iberian Peninsula. Muslims lived there from 711 to 1492, although their lands got smaller after the 11th century.
content.transferTask: Introduce a region you know with one contrast (although) and one end point (until).
content.teacherReflection: Did the time line make the 781 years clear, and did learners keep “Al-Andalus” and “Andalusia” apart?

exitTicket: Complete: “Al-Andalus was … Although …, Muslims lived there until …”

rubricLevels.secure: Gives the period and the meaning of Al-Andalus.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the first two sentences.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses although correctly.
Uses known as correctly.

content.chapter: Chapter 2: The Muslim Conquest of Spain
objectives: Retell the conquest in order with 711, 712 and “in just three years”.
Explain two kinds of reasons for the fast conquest.
Use due to / because of + noun and because + clause.
Explain a fast change in their own world with causes.
content.pedagogy: The chapter tells a story (who came, when, what they captured) and then explains it (why it was so easy). Keep the two jobs apart on the board: a time line on the left, a cause web on the right. Learners first secure the order, then the reasons.
priorKnowledge: Past simple of irregular verbs: began, came, moved.
The difference between because and because of may be new.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Tariq ibn Ziyad started the conquest; Musa ibn Nusayr joined him a year later. They were not the same person.
The book does not say the Muslims were invited by the Visigoths; it says unhappy people opened their gates.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: due to / because of + noun vs because + clause · passive “was made up of”, “were motivated by”
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort reasons into problems inside the kingdom and the people’s reaction.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose due to / because of / because, then correct three passive sentences.
Likely errors: *because the problems · *made up from · *who motivated by.
Use (Activity 4): five sentences about a fast change with two kinds of reasons.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: TA-riq ibn zi-YAD, MU-sa ibn nu-SAYR, to-LE-do, VIS-i-goths /ˈvɪzɪɡɒθs/, if-RI-qi-ya.
Stress: con-QUER-ors, de-TER-mined, vol-un-TAR-i-ly, SAV-iors.
beforeReading: Show the Strait of Gibraltar on a map. Ask: “Why do you think the conquest started here?” (Europe and Africa are very close.)
duringReading: First reading: Who started the conquest and when?
Build the time line 711 → 712 → three years.
Second reading: list the problems of the Visigothic Kingdom.
afterReading: Optional group task: “How Al-Andalus Began” jigsaw (Chapters 1–2).
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Map hook; 5–13 First reading and board time line; 13–20 Second reading: cause web (kingdom problems / people’s reaction); 20–24 Quick Challenge; 24–36 Language Focus Activities 1–3; 36–43 Use in pairs: a fast change in our town; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which problems did the Visigothic Kingdom have?
Why did many people see the Muslims as saviors?
Which reason do historians give in the last sentences?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Tariq ibn Ziyad” and “Open City Gates” when the picture is in place.
The group task “How Al-Andalus Began” fits after this chapter.
Word Notes: conquerors, determined, made up, captured, governor, conquered, due to, struggles, throne, unrest, voluntarily, saviors.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the time line with gaps (711 ____ / 712 ____ / three years ____) and the cause web with the two headings already written.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short news report from 714: “In just three years …”, using two passives and two reasons.

formativeAssessment: Puts the four events in order.
Separates causes inside Spain from the people’s reaction.
Uses because of + noun and because + clause correctly.
expectedResponses: Tariq ibn Ziyad started the conquest in 711 and captured Toledo. Musa ibn Nusayr joined him in 712. The conquest was fast due to the problems of the Visigothic Kingdom and because many people saw the Muslims as saviors.
content.transferTask: Explain a fast change in a team, school or town with one noun reason and one clause reason.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners keep the story order and the explanation apart, and did they use because / because of correctly?

exitTicket: Write two sentences: one with because of + noun and one with because + clause about the conquest.

rubricLevels.secure: Retells 711, 712 and three years in order.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the dates in the text.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains kingdom problems and the people’s reaction.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the two headings of the cause web.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses due to / because of / because correctly.

content.chapter: Chapter 3: A Cultural Golden Age
objectives: Give three pieces of evidence for the cultural golden age.
Explain why Al-Andalus had a unique culture.
Compare the urban Islamic community with the rural Christian society.
Use when + past continuous, far more … than and not only … but also.
content.pedagogy: The chapter argues a claim (a golden age) with numbers and names. Learners act as fact-checkers: Each claim on the board needs one piece of evidence from the text. The second paragraph is a comparison, so a T-chart (urban / rural) works well.
priorKnowledge: Comparatives and superlatives.
Past continuous for background.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The chapter does not say that Christians had no culture; it says they lived a simpler, rural life.
Ibn Jubayr was born in this period; he is not one of the thinkers in the list.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: when + past simple, past continuous background · far more … than / much + comparative / the biggest · not only did … but … also · while for contrast
Notice (Activity 1): background (was enjoying) and event (was born).
Build (Activities 2–3): complete the comparisons, then rewrite not only … but also and urban / rural with while.
Likely errors: *more prosperous that · *not only different cultures met (no inversion) · *was enjoy.
Use (Activity 4): five to six sentences about a golden age.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: ibn RUSHD, ibn tu-FAYL, ibn al-A-ra-bi, va-LEN-ci-a.
Stress: PROS-per-ous, U-nique /juˈniːk/, com-bi-NA-tion, UR-ban, RU-ral.
beforeReading: Ask: “What makes a city great: size, money, books, buildings?” Collect ideas.
duringReading: First reading: Find three numbers and say what they show.
Claim–evidence chart: golden age / unique culture / different systems.
Second reading: urban–rural T-chart.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: What makes a city great?; 5–14 First reading: numbers and names, claim–evidence chart; 14–20 Urban–rural T-chart; 20–24 Quick Challenge; 24–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: a golden age in pairs; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What evidence does the chapter give for a golden age?
Why was the culture of Al-Andalus unique?
How did the conquest change the Mediterranean Sea?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Córdoba” and “Thinkers of a Golden Age” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: prosperous, impressed, stood out, unique, combination, urban, rural.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the claim–evidence chart with the evidence already written but mixed up; learners match it to the claims.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a paragraph comparing Córdoba and a city you know, with three comparison forms.

formativeAssessment: Gives evidence with numbers or names.
Explains the mix of European, Asian and African traditions.
Uses a comparison and not only … but also correctly.
expectedResponses: Córdoba was the biggest city in Western Europe, Seville had 500 bathhouses, and brilliant thinkers like Ibn Rushd lived there. The culture was unique because it mixed European, Asian and African traditions.
content.transferTask: Describe a golden age of a place you know with evidence and one comparison.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners support each claim with evidence from the text rather than with general praise?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with far more … than and one with not only … but also about Al-Andalus.

rubricLevels.secure: Supports the golden age with facts from the text.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the numbers in paragraph 1.

rubricLevels.secure: Compares urban and rural correctly.
Uses far more … than and not only … but also.

content.chapter: Chapter 4: The Umayyad State in Al-Andalus
objectives: Explain why the Iberian Peninsula was the next step after North Africa.
Describe how the Umayyads started a new era in Al-Andalus.
List the groups in the population of Islamic Spain.
Use by + past perfect, for / until, consist of / make up.
content.pedagogy: Two short ideas: how the Umayyads arrived (a chain of dates) and who lived there (a list of groups). A date chain on the board (710 → 750 → 756 → 1031) and a population circle with seven groups give learners two clear visual anchors.
priorKnowledge: Past perfect may be new; past simple is secure.
The words Arab, Berber and Christian.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The Abbasids did not rule Al-Andalus; they overthrew the Umayyads in the East, and the Umayyads started a new era in Al-Andalus.
“Changed hands 19 times” means 19 rulers in turn, not 19 conquests by outsiders.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: by + date + past perfect · for + length / until + end point · therefore · consist of / make up / form · more numerous than
Notice (Activity 1): “By 710, Muslims had conquered …”.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose for / until / therefore, then rewrite with make up and more … than.
Likely errors: *By 710, Muslims conquered (unclear time) · *consisted from · *since 275 years.
Use (Activity 4): five sentences about a diverse group.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: UM-ay-yad /uˈmaɪjæd/, ab-BA-sids, abd al-rah-MAN.
Stress: o-ver-THREW, DI-verse /daɪˈvɜːrs/, CON-verts (noun) vs con-VERT (verb).
beforeReading: Write 750 and 756 on the board. Ask: “What could happen to a family that loses power in one place?”
duringReading: First reading: complete the date chain 710 → 750 → 756 → 1031.
Find how many times the throne changed hands.
Second reading: draw the population circle with seven groups.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Dates hook; 5–13 First reading: date chain; 13–20 Population circle in pairs; 20–24 Quick Challenge; 24–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: who lives here?; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why was Spain the natural next step?
What did rulers from Abd al-Rahman I to Abd al-Rahman III work for?
Which group became more numerous than the Arab Muslims?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “A New Umayyad Era” and “Many Peoples Together” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: marks, except for, towards, overthrew, changed hands, highly diverse, converts.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the date chain with the events on cards to place, and the population circle with first letters.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph: “How the Umayyads came to Al-Andalus”, using by + past perfect and therefore.

formativeAssessment: Completes the date chain correctly.
Names at least five groups.
Uses by + past perfect and consist of correctly.
expectedResponses: By 710 Muslims had conquered almost all of North Africa, so Spain was the next step. The Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads in 750, but the Umayyads started a new era in Al-Andalus in 756 and ruled for 275 years.
content.transferTask: Describe the people of a group you know with consist of and make up.
content.teacherReflection: Did the date chain help learners understand the past perfect “by 710”?

exitTicket: Complete: “By 710, Muslims had … The population of Islamic Spain consisted of …”

rubricLevels.secure: Orders 710, 750, 756 and 1031 with events.
Names the main groups of the population.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the last three sentences.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses by + past perfect and consist of.

content.chapter: Chapter 5: Abd al-Rahman III and the Golden Age
objectives: Explain three things Abd al-Rahman III did to make the state strong.
Explain why he claimed the title of caliph in 929.
Explain how he united different groups into “the Andalusians”.
Use to + verb, by + -ing, had to, whose and rather than.
content.pedagogy: This is a dense chapter about one ruler. A “leader’s plan” chart (aim → action → result) turns the long paragraphs into a clear argument. Learners then notice that the text itself uses purpose (to …) and method (by …-ing) language to build that plan.
priorKnowledge: To + verb for purpose.
The words caliph and tax.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The Fatimids announced their own caliphate in North Africa in 909; Abd al-Rahman III claimed the title in 929. They were rivals, not the same state.
The native Spanish people were tired of Arab nobility rather than Islamic rule: the book does not say they were against Islam.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: to + verb (purpose) · by + -ing (method) · had to · whose · rather than / instead of
Notice (Activity 1): sort purpose and method phrases.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose had to / whose / rather than, then rewrite with in order to and instead of + -ing.
Likely errors: *for lead · *by do this · *who arrogant attitude.
Use (Activity 4): a leader’s plan in five to six sentences.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: abd al-rah-MAN the THIRD, FA-ti-mids, con-stan-ti-NO-ple, has-DAY ibn sha-PRUT.
Stress: am-BAS-sa-dors, AT-ti-tude, no-BIL-i-ty.
beforeReading: Ask: “What does a new leader need to do to make a country strong?” Collect three ideas.
duringReading: First reading: complete the aim–action–result chart.
Find the years 929, 909 and 951 and what happened.
Second reading: how did he reduce the power of the Arab nobles?
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Leader hook; 5–15 First reading: aim–action–result chart in pairs; 15–20 Dates check; 20–24 Quick Challenge; 24–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: a leader’s plan; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did the northern Christian states pay a tax?
Why did foreign powers send ambassadors?
What happened after the Umayyad dynasty fell?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Caliph in 929” and “Ambassadors at Córdoba” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: launched, make peace, claimed, caliph, lead, ambassadors, boosted, reduce, attitude, ruining, nobles, nobility, split into, declared.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the actions already written; learners add the aim and result for each.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short speech by an ambassador at the court of Córdoba, describing three of the caliph’s actions with to and by.

formativeAssessment: Gives three actions with aims.
Explains how he reduced the nobles’ power.
Uses purpose and method forms correctly.
expectedResponses: He claimed the title of caliph to lead the Islamic world, made gold coins to compete in world trade, and gave positions to Christian slaves and Berbers. By doing this, he reduced the power of the Arab nobles and united the Andalusians.
content.transferTask: Describe a leader’s plan with purpose and method language.
content.teacherReflection: Did the chart help learners follow a dense chapter, and did they use to and by + -ing for different jobs?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with to + verb and one with by + -ing about Abd al-Rahman III.

rubricLevels.secure: Links actions with their aims.
Explains the new nation of Andalusians.
Uses to + verb and by + -ing.

content.chapter: Chapter 6: The Small Sultanates and the Reconquista
objectives: Explain why the small sultanates lost power after 1031.
Describe the meaning and steps of the Reconquista (Toledo 1085, Córdoba 1236).
Say when and where the Sultanate of Granada was founded.
Use make + person + verb, however / on the other hand and to + verb.
content.pedagogy: The chapter is a cause chain of weakness: division → alliances with rivals → loss of Toledo → crusade → loss of Córdoba. A falling-steps diagram on the board (each step lower) shows the direction of the story.
priorKnowledge: Past continuous for background.
The word alliance may be new.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The Reconquista was not one battle; it was a long process over centuries.
The Sultanate of Granada was founded during this chaos (1231); it was not the old Umayyad state.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: make + person + base verb · however / on the other hand · to + verb (purpose) · past continuous background (were fighting)
Notice (Activity 1): “Losing this important city finally made them realize …”.
Build (Activities 2–3): fill however / on the other hand / to, then correct three past forms.
Likely errors: *made them to realize · *did not saw · *losed.
Use (Activity 4): a group that lost strength.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: re-con-QUIS-ta /reɪˌkɒŋˈkiːstə/, cas-TILE, FER-di-nand.
Stress: al-LI-ance, ad-VAN-tage, re-AL-ize /ˈriːəlaɪz/.
beforeReading: Ask: “What happens to a team when the players stop working together?”
duringReading: First reading: build the falling-steps diagram (1031 → Toledo 1085 → crusade → Córdoba 1236).
Find who the rulers of Toledo made an alliance with.
Second reading: Why did the Muslim states still survive?
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Team hook; 5–14 First reading: falling-steps diagram; 14–20 Second reading questions; 20–24 Quick Challenge; 24–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: united or divided?; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What does “Reconquista” mean?
Why was the capture of Toledo a turning point?
Who helped the Muslim states survive?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Toledo, 1085” and “The Sultanate of Granada” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: made an alliance, Reconquista, realize, took on.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the falling-steps diagram with dates; learners match the events.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short report from 1085 by a Muslim adviser explaining the danger, using however and made + person + verb.

formativeAssessment: Explains division as the cause of weakness.
Gives Toledo 1085 and Córdoba 1236.
Uses made them realize correctly.
expectedResponses: After 1031 local rulers cared only about their own borders and even asked Christian kingdoms for help. This weakened them step by step. Losing Toledo in 1085 made them realize the danger of the Reconquista.
content.transferTask: Explain how a divided group lost strength.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see the chain of causes, not just a list of dates?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “made … realize” and one with “however” about the small sultanates.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains division and alliances.
Gives the main dates in order.
Uses made + person + verb and contrast linkers.

content.chapter: Chapter 7: The Fall of Granada
objectives: Name the turning points of 1248, 1469 and 1492.
Explain why the union of Aragon and Castile mattered.
Describe the life of Muslims in the Christian kingdoms after 1248.
Use there were still, with + noun, the passive and finally.
content.pedagogy: A very short chapter that closes the political history. Use a three-point time line and ask learners to give each point a title (“Seville falls”, “Two crowns, one house”, “The end of Islamic rule”). Naming the turning points helps them remember the whole arc of Chapters 2–7.
priorKnowledge: Passive past simple.
The words king, queen and marriage.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Not all Muslims left in 1248; many lived as peasants in the Christian kingdoms.
The 1469 marriage united two Christian kingdoms; it was not a marriage between a Muslim and a Christian ruler.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: there were still · with + noun (cause) · passive “were united” · finally
Notice (Activity 1): “there were still many Muslims living …”.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose with / were united / finally, then rewrite with because of and a passive.
Likely errors: *there was still many Muslims · *the kingdoms united under (missing passive) · *at finally.
Use (Activity 4): three turning points in a history learners know.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: AR-a-gon, cas-TILE, CATH-o-lic MON-archs /ˈmɒnərks/.
Stress: u-ni-fi-CA-tion, PEAS-ants /ˈpezənts/.
beforeReading: Ask: “What can change when two countries become one?”
duringReading: First reading: three dates, three events.
Give each turning point a title.
Second reading: How did Muslims live in the Christian kingdoms?
afterReading: Review the time line of Chapters 2–7.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading: three-point time line; 12–18 Titles for the turning points in pairs; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–34 Language Focus 1–3; 34–42 Use: three turning points; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What happened to Muslims after Seville was captured?
Why was 1469 a major turning point?
What ended in 1492?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Seville, 1248” and “Aragon and Castile” when the picture is in place.
This chapter has no Word Notes.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the three years with the events on cards.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Make a full time line of Chapters 2–7 with one sentence from the book for each date.

formativeAssessment: Orders the three turning points.
Explains the union of the kingdoms.
Uses there were still correctly.
expectedResponses: Seville fell in 1248, but there were still many Muslims in the Christian kingdoms. In 1469 the marriage of the Catholic Monarchs united Aragon and Castile. Finally, in 1492, the last Muslim kingdom fell.
content.transferTask: Describe three turning points in a history learners know.
content.teacherReflection: Could learners connect this short chapter to the whole political story?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “there were still” and one with “finally” about this chapter.

rubricLevels.secure: Orders 1248, 1469 and 1492 with events.
Explains what the union changed.
Uses there were still and finally.

content.chapter: Chapter 8: The Inquisition and Forced Conversion
objectives: Describe the choice Muslims faced after 1492.
Explain why the Inquisition was established in 1499.
Order the laws that targeted Islamic culture.
Use were forced to, so … that, must be + past participle and sequence words.
content.pedagogy: This is the hardest chapter of the book emotionally. Keep the focus on what the text reports and on the idea of identity (language, names, food, clothes, baths). A “steps” chart with the writer’s own sequence words lets learners see the policy grow without retelling every detail.
priorKnowledge: Passive forms; must.
The words church, mosque and religion.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The text describes a government and church policy of the time; it is not about Christians or Spanish people today.
At first the government tried to persuade; the strict laws came later because church leaders became impatient.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: were forced to + verb · so + adjective + that · must be + past participle · sequence words (first, soon after, finally, on top of that) · as a result
Notice (Activity 1): sort the laws into earlier and later steps.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite cause and result with so and because.
Likely errors: *were forced choose · *such strong that · *must sent.
Use (Activity 4): what makes up an identity, with respect.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: in-qui-SI-tion /ˌɪŋkwɪˈzɪʃən/, HA-lal, BAP-tized.
Stress: per-SUADE, e-LIM-i-nate, cir-cum-CI-sion, MON-as-ter-ies.
beforeReading: Ask: “What makes you feel part of your community: your language, your name, your food?” Collect ideas without discussing the chapter yet.
duringReading: First reading: What choice did Muslims face?
Find why church leaders became impatient.
Second reading: list the laws in the order the writer gives them.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Identity hook; 5–13 First reading: the choice and the reason for the Inquisition; 13–20 Steps chart with sequence words; 20–24 Quick Challenge; 24–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: what makes up an identity; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: How did life change for Muslims after 1492?
Why did the church leaders become impatient?
Why do you think baths were a target?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Granada, 1499” and “Public Baths” when the picture is in place.
Read this chapter calmly. Allow learners to ask questions, and keep answers within what the book says.
Word Notes: exile, separate, persuade, Inquisition, eliminate, banned, circumcision, properly, destroy, demanded.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the steps chart with the sequence words already written on the left.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph explaining why language and names are important for identity, using so … that and as a result.

formativeAssessment: Describes the choice and the Inquisition correctly.
Orders the laws with sequence words.
Uses were forced to and so … that correctly.
expectedResponses: After 1492 Muslims were forced to choose between becoming Christian and leaving. Church leaders thought the process was too slow, so they established the Inquisition in 1499. First, halal butcher shops were closed; soon after, Arabic became illegal.
content.transferTask: Explain what makes up a community’s identity and how we can respect it.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners stay with the text and keep the discussion respectful?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “were forced to” and one with “so … that” about this chapter.

rubricLevels.secure: Describes the choice and the Inquisition.
Orders the laws with sequence words.
Uses were forced to and so … that.

content.chapter: Chapter 9: Ottoman Aid and the Final Exile
objectives: Explain what Bayezid II did in 1487 and in 1502.
Explain what Ahmed I did between 1609 and 1614 and why he could not do more.
Say what happened to the Muslims of Spain after 1526.
Use could not … because, too busy with, in response, thanks to and managed to.

metadata.title: Al-Andalus B1 — Teacher’s Book
metadata.subtitle: Al-Andalus: Spain under Islamic Rule (711–1492)
metadata.estimatedDuration: 13 chapter units of 45 minutes each. Whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow connected historical texts with dates, names, causes and results, and who can produce supported explanations and short reflections.
metadata.purpose: Develop evidence-based B1 reading, listening, speaking and writing through the history of Al-Andalus: its conquest, golden age, society, economy, science and legacy, and its end, using the Language Focus attached to every story chapter.
metadata.approachDesc: Every story chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning and evidence; the Quick Challenge checks comprehension. Grammar is then learned inductively: in the Language Focus, learners first NOTICE a form in a real chapter sentence and work out what it does, then BUILD it in controlled, meaningful practice, and finally USE it in connected YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world. Chapters with many names and dates use time lines, charts and maps so that learners organize facts before they discuss them.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 13 Quick Challenges, text-evidence checks, chapter Language Focus tasks (Notice → Build → Use), exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and Final Challenge.

formative: Short spoken and written Use tasks

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs: a short question, a map, a date or a picture.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist (when the audio is ready), then read and follow the chapter’s own evidence structure: time line, cause and result, contrast, groups of people or a list of facts.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (notice → build → use), then a connected B1 transfer about the learners’ own world. Long chapters can be divided into two 40-minute lessons.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Word Notes are the bold words of the teacher-approved text. Prioritise them and the linking words that carry the chapter’s causes, results and contrasts.
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context, a map or a picture before any direct explanation.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse vocabulary in Language Focus production, exit tickets and the cumulative review.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based. Start from the story sentence, ask a meaning question (What does this form tell us?), let learners formulate the rule in their own words, then confirm it and practise it in context. Rule explanations appear in the app only after learners answer. Do not replace the chapter work with unrelated grammar drills.
grammarSequence: Ch1: although + clause · until · was/is known as · the most … that … had ever seen
Ch2: due to / because of + noun vs because + clause · passive “was made up of”, “were motivated by”
Ch3: when + past simple, past continuous background · far more … than / much + comparative / the biggest · not only did … but … also · while for contrast
Ch4: by + date + past perfect · for + length / until + end point · therefore · consist of / make up / form · more numerous than
Ch5: to + verb (purpose) · by + -ing (method) · had to · whose · rather than / instead of
Ch6: make + person + base verb · however / on the other hand · to + verb (purpose) · past continuous background (were fighting)
Ch7: there were still · with + noun (cause) · passive “were united” · finally
Ch8: were forced to + verb · so + adjective + that · must be + past participle · sequence words (first, soon after, finally, on top of that) · as a result
Ch9: could not … because · too busy with + noun · in response · thanks to · manage to + verb · ask someone not to + verb
Ch10: were allowed to · in return · live like · relative which / who · for this reason · the only exception was
Ch11: when + clause · in addition · however · in + place + alone · passive (were exported, were brought)
Ch12: while + past continuous (contrast) · thanks to · it is known that · translate into · passive (were brought back)
Ch13: was built by · comes from · so much that · inspired / was inspired by · was translated into

skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: follow narration for gist, dates, causes, results and key details.
skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: identify main ideas, direct evidence, time lines, cause-result chains, contrast and lists of facts.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: explain causes and results, compare periods and groups, and transfer chapter language respectfully.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: produce connected B1 paragraphs using evidence, linking words and chapter patterns.

valuesFocus: D14 Respect — Respect for people of different faiths and backgrounds who lived together.
D1 Justice — Fair treatment and the right to keep one’s faith and identity.
D20 Helpfulness — Helping people in need, even from far away.
D3 Diligence — Hard work in science, trade, farming and building.
languageFocus: Every one of the 13 chapters has a Language Focus set built as Notice → Build → Use (4 activities).
Use the Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence and ask a meaning question before naming the form.
The Use step is connected spoken or written production about a new, non-story situation.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the reasoning target: one paragraph at a time, a time line or chart given in part, selected vocabulary, audio replay, sentence frames and oral rehearsal. Extend by combining more chapter patterns or adding a second piece of evidence, not by introducing outside facts.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful teaching
notes: Keep explanations within the wording of the book; do not add outside details, legends or opinions.

Chapters 8 and 9 (the Inquisition, forced conversion and exile) are hard to read. Discuss them calmly and factually. The text describes a policy of that time; it is not about Christians or Spanish people today.
Discuss wars, conquests and defeats factually and without sensationalism; never role-play violence.
Treat all faiths with respect. Convivencia is supported with evidence from the text, not with general praise.
Bracketed Turkish names in the text belong to the teacher-approved story; they are read as they are.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: The story of Al-Andalus links a medieval history with questions every community faces: how people of different faiths can live together, how knowledge travels between cultures, and how a community’s identity can be respected.

themes.title: Living together:
themes.description: Muslims, Christians and Jews lived and worked together in Al-Andalus (Chapter 10). Discuss what helps diverse communities live together today.

themes.title: Knowledge without borders:
themes.description: Knowledge flowed from Baghdad and Cairo through Al-Andalus to Europe, and translators of three faiths worked together (Chapter 12). Compare this with how scientists share knowledge today.

themes.title: Identity and respect:
themes.description: Chapter 8 shows how language, names, food and clothes make up an identity. Discuss how we can respect the identity of people around us.

themes.title: Help from far away:
themes.description: Chapter 9 shows how people tried to help others in another country. Connect this with how communities help people affected by disasters or conflict today.

actions: Learn and use a greeting in a language spoken by a classmate or neighbor.
Make a short poster about one scientist from Al-Andalus and one thing we still use today.
Find one local charity and write two sentences about what it does.

reflectivePrompt.desc: The Arabized Christians spoke Arabic and Latin and became a bridge between cultures (Chapter 10). Write six to eight sentences about a person you know who connects different groups of people. What do they do, and what happens as a result?

metadata.whoIsThisFor: B1 learners who study the history of Al-Andalus alone or with a teacher.
learningGoals: Find evidence in the text before answering.
Follow dates, names, causes and results across seven centuries.
Explain what made Al-Andalus special and how it ended, with evidence.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in connected sentences.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Read (and listen, when the audio is ready) before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 13.

readingDiary.intro: Keep this diary when you finish the book. Write short answers.
prompts: The date I finished the book:
My favorite chapter, and one reason:
One fact about Al-Andalus that surprised me:
One sentence for a friend: “Read this book because …”
One new word I want to keep:
The next book I want to read in the library:

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 13 chapters. Plan the whole book before Chapter 1.
points: Choose your study days and how many chapters you will read each week.
Write one personal goal for this book.
Save new words to My words and review them after one day, three days and one week.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 25 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and the “Before You Read” question.
Read for the main idea.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Read and Listen
sections.text: Read every chapter twice: once for the main idea, once for the details. When the audio is ready, listen once while you follow the text.
points: First reading: What is the chapter about?
Second reading: Mark names, dates and linking words.
Say one long sentence aloud with the right pauses.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes
sections.text: Bold words have Word Notes. Use them after you have tried to understand the sentence yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Write the word in a new sentence of your own.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Answer before you read the feedback. If you are wrong, repair the answer with the text.
points: Find the paragraph the question is about.
Read the key sentence again.
Explain why the right answer is right, then try again.

sections.title: 6. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has 4 Language Focus activities built from the chapter’s own sentences.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): Look at a sentence and what it means.
Activities 2–3 (Build): Choose, complete, correct or rewrite forms.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say connected sentences about a different situation.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Some chapters have many names and dates. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Read one paragraph only.
Make a time line of the dates.
List the names and what each one did.
Learn only three words today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Book
sections.text: The book shows respect, justice, helpfulness and hard work. Find the sentence first, then think of a small action of your own.
points: Respect: Respect: Muslims, Christians and Jews lived and worked together in Al-Andalus (Chapter 10).
Justice: Justice: Christians kept their religion and property under the agreements, while later laws took away the identity of Muslims (Chapters 8 and 10).
Helpfulness: Helpfulness: Bayezid II and Ahmed I tried to help the Muslims of Al-Andalus in different ways (Chapter 9).
Diligence: Diligence: Scholars, farmers, textile makers and builders created the wealth and knowledge of Al-Andalus (Chapters 11–13).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 13, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Knowledge Check
Vocabulary Challenge
Master Glossary
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back
sections.text: Before Chapter 1 and again at the end, answer the “I can” statements of a few chapters. What can you do now that you could not do before?
points: Which chapter changed what you knew?
Tell the story of Al-Andalus in five sentences to someone at home, in your home language or in English.
